Title Defense · Group DJANGO
BS CS – Data Science · FEU Tech

Fish feeds our families and supports coastal livelihoods.

Fishers, vendors and businesses depend on a steady supply.

Can past data warn us when that supply will fall short?

00
Our proposed study
AquaTerra:
Forecasting Municipal Fish Landing Shortfalls and Estimating Gross Landing Value at Risk in Selected Philippine Coastal Provinces
Key terms · click
Municipal
Catch from municipal waters, up to 15 km from shore (RA 10654, 2015), by fishers with no boat or boats of 3 gross tons or less.
Landings
Fish brought ashore, in tonnes, per province and quarter (PSA, 2026).
Quarter
Q1 Jan–Mar · Q2 Apr–Jun · Q3 Jul–Sep · Q4 Oct–Dec.
Gross landing value at risk
Projected shortfall × historical first-sale price. Gross value at stake, not income, profit or damage.
Fish feeds our families and supports the livelihoods of coastal communities. [→] Behind every catch are fishers, vendors and businesses that depend on a steady supply. [→] Can historical fisheries and environmental data help us anticipate when that supply will fall short? [→] Good day, respected panelists. We are Group Django, and today we present our proposed study, 'AquaTerra: Forecasting Municipal Fish Landing Shortfalls and Estimating Gross Landing Value at Risk in Selected Philippine Coastal Provinces.' 'Municipal' fish means catch from municipal waters, up to 15 km from shore under RA 8550 as amended by RA 10654, by fishers using no boat or boats of three gross tons or less. 'Landings' means the catch brought ashore, in tonnes per province per quarter. (Click a key term to define it; press Q for panel questions.)
01
I · Background

Fish supports coastal towns,
and supply is falling.

1 · Why it matters

Fisheries are key to food security and livelihoods.

FAO (2024)

2023 oil spill, Naujan, Oriental Mindoro: fishing banned, income lost.

Agaton et al. (2023)
2 · The decline
~45Mkg / year

National capture fisheries, linked to overfishing and illegal fishing.

Oceana (2026)
3 · Forecasting so far

A regional forecasting model for Philippine fisheries, with environmental data.

Bokingkito et al. (2026)

Our starting point.

The question  Can we see these drops coming, province by province?
When fish gets expensive at the palengke, it's usually because less fish came in. Fish isn't just food on our table; it supports jobs and income in coastal towns, and FAO points to fisheries as key to food security and livelihoods (FAO, 2024). [→] We've seen what happens when supply is disrupted. After the February 2023 oil spill off Naujan, Oriental Mindoro, fishing was banned; the fisherfolk interviewed lost their main income, some up to about US$1,300 a week, and relief did not cover basic needs (Agaton et al., 2023). [→] And the long-term trend is worrying: Oceana reports capture fisheries fell from about 2.6M mt in 2010 to 1.9M in 2023, roughly 45M kg lost every year, a national figure (Oceana, 2026). Oceana links the decline to governance gaps: overfishing, illegal fishing, commercial vessels entering municipal waters and weak enforcement. [→] So can we see these drops coming? Bokingkito et al. (2026) built a regional forecasting model for Philippine fisheries using environmental data. That's our starting point. [→] So what's still missing?
02
II · Research Gaps

What existing forecasts leave open.

Existing forecasts work at region and sector level and stop at how much fish to expect. Bokingkito et al. (2026)
AquaTerra  turns forecasts into shortfalls and their value, province by province.
So here's what those studies already did. Existing forecasts like Bokingkito et al. (2026) work at the region and sector level, and they stop at how much fish to expect. [→] Gap 1: there are no seasonal shortfall forecasts by province and fish category, the level where local offices plan. We will forecast each province and fish category and flag seasonal shortfalls. [→] Gap 2: forecasts give kilos, not value. We will attach a historical first-sale price to each shortfall, using PSA value and volume records (PSA, 2026). [→] Gap 3: shortfall flags and value rankings haven't been checked. We will test how accurate the flags are, and whether the rankings hold when prices change, on later quarters the model has not seen (Hewamalage et al., 2023). [→] Gap 4: typhoons, rainfall and sea temperature are often linked to lower catch (Noy et al., 2023; Holmes et al., 2021), but few studies check whether they improve a provincial forecast. We will test that, and report it if they don't help. This is prediction, not cause. [→] That's where AquaTerra fits: it fills the gap by turning forecasts into shortfalls and their value at province level. (Press R for the references behind each gap.)
03
III · Statement of the Problem ↔ Specific Objectives

Initial questions, paired one-to-one.

General objective  AquaTerra will forecast next-quarter municipal fish landings, flag seasonal shortfalls and estimate their gross landing value at risk for five MIMAROPA provinces.
Random Forest will rank and select the predictors. Nesslage et al. (2021)
GAMM will forecast landings with smooth curves. Holmes et al. (2021)
Initial research questions (preliminary)
Specific objectives
Our general objective: AquaTerra will forecast next-quarter municipal fish landings, flag seasonal shortfalls and estimate their gross landing value at risk for the five MIMAROPA provinces. Two algorithms, in one line each. Random Forest, many decision trees voting, will rank the candidate predictors and keep the useful ones (Nesslage et al., 2021). GAMM, a generalized additive mixed model, will add smooth curves for each selected predictor, plus province and fish-category effects, to forecast landings (Holmes et al., 2021). These are our initial research questions; we expect to refine them. Each is paired with exactly one specific objective. [→] SOP 1: What seasonal benchmarks will identify landing shortfalls for each MIMAROPA province and fish category, using PSA quarterly records from 2002 to 2025? SO 1: to build seasonal benchmarks for each province × fish category from PSA quarterly landings, 2002 Q1–2025 Q4. [→] SOP 2: How much will prior typhoon exposure, rainfall and sea surface temperature improve next-quarter landing forecasts from a Random Forest–GAMM workflow? SO 2: to develop the Random Forest → GAMM workflow and measure the added value of typhoon, rainfall and SST predictors (with vs without). [→] SOP 3: What gross landing value at risk will the projected shortfalls carry when priced at historical first-sale prices? SO 3: to estimate the gross landing value at risk of each projected shortfall using historical first-sale prices, and rank the combinations. [→] SOP 4: How accurate will the forecasts be on held-out quarters (2022 Q2–2025 Q4), measured by MAE, RMSE and MASE against a seasonal-naive baseline? SO 4: to evaluate the forecasts on held-out quarters (2022 Q2–2025 Q4) with MAE, RMSE and MASE vs the seasonal-naive baseline, plus price-sensitivity and ranking-stability checks. The dashboard and the consultation with DTI or a fisheries agency are part of our scope, not separate objectives. (Click a row to highlight its pair.)

IV · Scope and Limitation

What we will cover, and what we won't claim.

Scope
✓
Study area · MIMAROPAOccidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, Palawan · 31 fish categories PSA (2026)
✓
Municipal fishCatch within municipal waters, up to 15 km from shore; boats of 3 gross tons or less RA 10654 (2015)
✓
Public data · 2002 Q1 – 2025 Q4PSA OpenSTAT · NASA IMERG · NOAA OISST · NOAA IBTrACS
✓
Forecast → shortfall → valueNext-quarter RF → GAMM forecasts, seasonal shortfalls, gross landing value at risk
✓
Evaluation & dashboard70/15/15 time split · web dashboard · consultation sought with DTI or a fisheries agency
Limitation · click to focus
Scope. Our study area will be MIMAROPA: Occidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon and Palawan, across the 31 named fish categories in PSA's marine municipal fisheries tables (PSA, 2026); PSA's 'Others' group will be left out. Municipal fish means catch within municipal waters, which under RA 8550 as amended by RA 10654 extend up to 15 km from the coastline, by fishers using no boat or boats of three gross tons or less (RA 10654, 2015). We will use public data from 2002 Q1 to 2025 Q4: PSA OpenSTAT, NASA IMERG, NOAA OISST and NOAA IBTrACS. Random Forest will select predictors and GAMM will forecast the next quarter; we will compare forecasts with seasonal benchmarks, value shortfalls with historical first-sale prices, evaluate on a 70/15/15 time split, show results on a web dashboard, and seek consultation with DTI or a relevant fisheries agency. [→] Limitations: selected provinces and marine municipal categories only; no commercial, aquaculture or inland fisheries and no field monitoring. Next quarter only; data gaps and delays may affect accuracy, and fishing effort and fuel costs will not be modeled. We will not establish causal effects of typhoons, rainfall or sea temperature. Gross landing value at risk will use historical prices, not income, profit or damage. The dashboard will be a research prototype, and adoption is not guaranteed.

Forecasts MAE · RMSE · MASE vs seasonal-naive
Value at risk price sensitivity · ranking stability
Hyndman & Athanasopoulos (2021); Hewamalage et al. (2023)
This slide is the whole data side of AquaTerra. [Stage 1] We will use four public datasets from 2002 Q1 to 2025 Q4. PSA OpenSTAT will give quarterly marine municipal landings and production value for the five MIMAROPA provinces and 31 fish categories (PSA, 2026). NASA IMERG will give rainfall (Huffman et al., 2023), NOAA OISST sea surface temperature (Huang et al., 2021), and NOAA IBTrACS typhoon tracks (Gahtan et al., 2024). [→ Stage 2] We will line everything up into one table: one row per province, fish category and quarter, with landings, landings in the same quarter last year, rainfall, sea temperature and recent typhoons. Price will be kept aside for the valuation step only; it will never be a predictor. Values shown are illustrative. [→ Stage 3] We will split the 96 quarters by time, 70/15/15, never shuffled. Train: 2002 Q1 to 2018 Q3, 67 quarters. Tune: 2018 Q4 to 2022 Q1, 14 quarters. Test: 2022 Q2 to 2025 Q4, 15 quarters, locked until the final check. The first year has no lag-4 value, so those rows will drop from training. Keeping selection and tuning inside earlier data follows Hewamalage et al. (2023); the 70/15/15 ratio is our design choice. (Click a segment to highlight its rows.) [→ Stage 4] We will score forecasts only on the Test quarters with MAE, RMSE and MASE against a seasonal-naive baseline, the same quarter last year (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021). For value at risk we will check price sensitivity and whether the rankings stay stable.

Gross value at stake, not profit or income. Rankings will be re-checked under each price.

Now the two algorithms and how they work together. [Stage 5] Random Forest is an ensemble of decision trees. It will learn only from the Train quarters, and we will rank predictors by permutation importance: if shuffling a predictor makes the error rise, it matters. Random Forest picks predictors; it does not make the final forecast. Using Random Forest importance to guide a GAMM follows Nesslage et al. (2021). Bars are illustrative. [→ Stage 6] GAMM, a generalized additive mixed model, will build the forecast by adding smooth curves for the season, lagged landings and each selected predictor, plus random effects for province and fish category, so groups can differ without separate models. GAMs have been used to forecast quarterly landings with environmental covariates (Holmes et al., 2021). Toggle 'Without' to see the comparison model: we will fit both, with and without typhoons, rainfall and sea temperature, and compare them on the Test quarters. If the weather terms don't help, we will report that. This is prediction, not cause. [→ Stage 7] Each next-quarter forecast will be compared with the seasonal benchmark, the usual level for that province, category and quarter. If the forecast is below it, the gap is the projected shortfall. Numbers are illustrative. [→ Stage 8] Shortfall tonnes times 1,000 times the historical first-sale price gives the gross landing value at risk, in pesos. We will rank province–category combinations, then swap to a unit-value proxy price and check whether the ranking holds. It is gross value at stake, not profit or income. Values are illustrative.

[→] BFAR could use the findings as supplementary information for monitoring and planning. [→] DTI could use exposure estimates in consultations with fisheries-related enterprises. [→] Fisherfolk associations and cooperatives could use seasonal supply outlooks for marketing and delivery coordination. [→] Traders, vendors and processors could use projected shortfalls for sourcing and inventory planning. "How will you separate prediction from causation?"

1 · The test we will run
Model Apast landings + season
vs
Model BA + typhoons + rain + SST
→
Test quartersMAE, RMSE, MASE
→
More accurate?= useful for prediction only
2 · Why accuracy is not proof

Other factors can move with the weather and change landings:

Fishing effortFuel pricesRegulationsReporting

Proving cause needs controlled or field studies, outside our scope.

3 · How we will word results
✓ "Typhoon exposure improves forecast accuracy here."
✕ "Typhoons cause lower landings."

Same rule for rainfall, SST and any top-ranked predictor.

We will test whether environmental information improves forecast accuracy. We will compare a model with only past landings and seasonality against one with typhoon exposure, rainfall and sea temperature added, both evaluated on the held-out Test quarters. The gap: typhoons, rainfall and sea temperature are often linked to lower catch (Noy et al., 2023; Holmes et al., 2021), but few studies check whether they improve a provincial forecast. We will test that, and report it if they don't help. That is prediction, not cause. [→] Better accuracy will mean predictive usefulness only. Fishing effort, fuel prices, regulations and reporting changes can move together with typhoons and weather and also affect landings. Proving cause would need controlled or field studies, which are outside our scope. [→] So our results will say 'improves forecast accuracy', [→] never 'causes'.

Ranking · price check
Gross landing value: for each province and quarter, we will multiply the tonnes landed in each fish category by the matching historical first-sale price for the same period and province. [→] Value at risk will work on the shortfall only: the seasonal benchmark minus the forecast, when the forecast is below it; otherwise zero. [→] We will multiply the shortfall in tonnes, times 1,000 for kilograms, by the matching price. That is the gross landing value at risk: gross value at stake, not profit or household income loss. Where first-sale prices are missing, we will use unit-value proxies (production value divided by volume; PSA, 2026). [→] Then we will rank the province–category combinations and check whether the ranking holds when we switch price source or move the price up or down. Values are illustrative.
